final_proof:
Regard the mass of the body as a nonnegative mass measure \(dm\) on three-dimensional Euclidean space. Its total mass is
\[
M=\int_B dm,
\]
and, writing \(c\) for its centre of mass,
\[
\int_B (x-c)\,dm(x)=0.
\]
(For a system of point masses, the integrals below are simply the corresponding sums.)

Choose a unit vector \(u\) in the common direction of the parallel axes. Since \(A\) passes through \(c\), it can be written
\[
A=\{c+tu:t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
There is a unique vector \(a\) perpendicular to \(u\) such that
\[
A'=\{c+a+tu:t\in\mathbb R\}.
\]
Indeed, if one starts with any vector joining a point of \(A\) to a point of \(A'\), its component perpendicular to \(u\) is this vector \(a\). Consequently \(\lVert a\rVert=l\), the distance between the two axes.

Let \(P(v)=v-(v\cdot u)u\) be orthogonal projection onto the plane perpendicular to \(u\). The squared distance from a point \(x\) to \(A\) is \(\lVert P(x-c)\rVert^2\), whereas its squared distance to \(A'\) is
\[
\lVert P(x-c-a)\rVert^2.
\]
Because \(a\perp u\), we have \(P(a)=a\). Hence
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{dist}(x,A')^2
 &=\lVert P(x-c)-a\rVert^2\\
 &=\lVert P(x-c)\rVert^2-2a\cdot P(x-c)+\lVert a\rVert^2\\
 &=\operatorname{dist}(x,A)^2-2a\cdot(x-c)+l^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
In the last equality we used \(a\perp u\), which implies \(a\cdot P(x-c)=a\cdot(x-c)\).

Integrating this identity against the mass measure and using the definition of moment of inertia gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
I
 &=\int_B\operatorname{dist}(x,A')^2\,dm(x)\\
 &=\int_B\operatorname{dist}(x,A)^2\,dm(x)
   -2a\cdot\int_B(x-c)\,dm(x)
   +l^2\int_Bdm(x)\\
 &=I_0-2a\cdot0+l^2M
 =I_0+Ml^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Thus \(I=I_0+Ml^2\), as claimed.
